tags: hill top, enclosure, burning, animal sacrifice, votive lake
description:
Located in the Westmeath lakelands, the Hill of Uisneach is one of the primary Royal Centres of Irish medieval tradition, boasting evidence of near-continuous activity from the Neolithic through the Bronze, Iron, and Medieval periods. The site remains a significant landscape featuring a ruined cromlech, natural springs, multi-period enclosures, and the massive limestone boulder known as the Cat Stone. Although the site fell out of use after the medieval period, since the 20th century it has served as a political and religious gathering place.

Formal archaeological excavations on the hilltop have been limited. The most extensive study occurred in the 1920s and focused on the figure-of-eight enclosure known as Rathnew, though the lack of modern techniques at the time has made the findings difficult to interpret. Recent re-analysis suggests that Rathnew originated as a circular enclosure and a Late Iron Age cult centre, possibly dating from the 2nd century CE based on the presence of Roman finds. Evidence discovered at the site indicates animal sacrifice, large-scale burning of offerings, and the deposition of articulated animal remains.

The visible figure-of-eight enclosure appears to have been constructed around this older cult centre during the 7th or 8th century CE, around the time Clann Cholmáin annexed the Westmeath lakelands. Much like Tara and Navan Fort, the site likely appropriated the authority of the ancient cult centre to establish a centre of royal power, which remained in use until at least the 12th century. To the north of this enclosure lies Lough Lugh, which the _dindshenchas_ tradition identifies as the location where the god Lugh was drowned. His burial place is traditionally cited as Carn Lugdach, a Bronze Age cairn situated just to the east of the lake.

Modern morphological analysis has identified a large enclosure surrounding this cairn, suggesting it is a late antique feature contemporary with the Rathnew cult centre to the south. While the lake is partially man-made and was cleared of silt some time before the medieval period, some scholars suggest it served as a votive lake similar to the King’s Stables at Navan. However, no material evidence has been recovered, as any existing artifacts may have been destroyed during the artificial clearing of the lake.

Historical evidence from the late 7th-century tract _Tucait Baile Mongáin_ indicates that a major assembly, or _mór dál_, would convene at Uisneach during that era. Scholars such as Schott have argued that this gathering functioned as an _óenach_, a traditional festival and assembly. Gleeson further supports this by comparing the large enclosure surrounding Carn Lugdach to similar structures at Rathcroghan, suggesting it was the likely focal point for these significant tribal and royal assemblies.
